title: Product photography for a jewelry studio
metaTitle: Photograph jewelry for detail and size
excerpt: Photograph jewelry for detail, size, and care, in one crop and one background. Mixed crops make a careful studio look unfinished online.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table, sorting a consistent set of jewelry pictures.
caption: A table where a set of pictures gets checked as one grid. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which three photographs does a jewelry piece need?
faqs.answer: Shoot the whole piece for the grid, one detail that answers what a buyer would zoom toward, and one scale frame using the same reference every time. Photograph variants separately when they look different. Delete soft frames and any frame on a different background.

faqs.question: How should metal color be handled in the files?
faqs.answer: Choose a background that lets both gold and silver read, and keep the white balance steady. Check the file against the real piece in daylight before you publish. A heavy grade that makes every metal the same color is a false description.

faqs.question: What belongs in the alt text of a jewelry photo?
faqs.answer: Name the metal, the type of object, and the view, such as the whole piece or the detail of a setting. The scale frame should say it is on a hand if that is what it shows. A generic label like gold ring is too thin when the page is about a specific band.

markdown:
A jewelry studio product photography set has to carry detail, size, and the care of the object. The piece is small, the price is considered, and a muddy thumbnail will make it look cheap or, worse, unclear. Shoot every piece into the same crop and the same background so the grid reads as one studio. Mixed crops are how a careful bench starts to look like a flea market online.

The pictures are part of the facts. A beautiful frame that hides the scale is a kind of exaggeration. Treat that as a defect, the way you would treat a scratched shank.

## Three jobs, three distances

Plan three distances and use them on purpose.

- The whole piece, large enough to recognize, small enough to show the full silhouette.
- A detail, close enough to judge a surface, a setting, or a joint.
- A scale frame: on a body, in a hand, or beside a reference you always use.

The grid uses the whole piece. The page uses all three. If you only publish the detail, every object becomes a texture and nobody knows whether they are buying a stud or a statement. If you only publish a wide lifestyle scene, the metal is a guess and the detail you spent the week on is invisible.

Shoot the piece, not the mood around it. Fabric, flowers, and handwritten notes can appear in one campaign image if you truly want one. They should not be the system. The system is the object on a ground that does not compete, lit so the metal reads as the metal you sell.

Keep the camera square to the piece for the grid frame. An extreme angle changes the apparent size from one ring to the next. You can use a second angle on the page when a clasp, a hinge, or a profile is part of the decision. Label it in the alt text and in the caption so it is a view, not a different product.

## Detail without losing the object

Detail is where studios overshoot. A macro so tight that the frame is a blur of prongs tells a jeweler something and tells a buyer nothing. Step back until the detail has an edge: the setting inside the ring, the clasp at the end of a chain, the place two metals meet.

Focus on the plane that matters. If the stone is the point, the stone is sharp. If the engraving is the point, the letters are sharp. A dreamy falloff across the only fact on the page is a portrait technique used in the wrong place.

Show the finish you will ship. If you photograph a piece before the final polish, you will sell a finish you do not deliver. Photograph the piece in the state that leaves the bench. If you offer two finishes, they are two pictures or two clearly marked states, not one frame and a dropdown that says "also available in matte."

Clean the piece. Fingerprints, dust, and a cloth fiber read enormous at this scale. Build a minute of cleaning into the shot, with the cloth you actually use, so the care is real and the file is clean. Do not "fix" a scratch in software that will still be on the ring. The picture is a promise about the object.

Reflections are information. A flat, dead metal can look like a render. A blown-out highlight can hide a prong. Move the light until the surface has shape and the edges are intact. You are allowed to look at the frame on a phone before you accept it. That is where the highlight will clip, if it clips.

## Scale that a stranger can use

Every piece page needs a way to judge size without having held it. Pick one scale method and repeat it so the shop becomes comparable.

A hand from the same person, shot the same way, is enough for many earrings and pendants. A ring on a finger needs the finger described, or a measurement beside it, because fingers differ. A simple matte bar or a coin, used every time, is more honest than a new prop each week. Choose one and put it in the shot list.

Photograph the size variants you sell if they look different at a glance. Two chain lengths, two hoop diameters. Writing the millimeter difference under a single frame asks the buyer to do work the picture should have done.

Weight is not visible, so do not pretend a photograph can carry it. The page copy carries grams. The picture's job is to avoid lying about bulk. A light piece shot to look massive will come back. A heavy piece shot only in extreme close-up will surprise someone who wanted delicate.

Consistently underexposing to look expensive is a style, and it fails scale and detail at once. Metal color shifts. Edges disappear. If the piece is pale gold, let it be pale. The luxury is the object, not a brown filter.

## Care, shown without costume

Care is in the handling. A piece photographed on a filthy bench says one thing. A piece floating in an impossible render says another. You want the middle: a real object, treated calmly.

The bench can appear when it teaches something: a setting in progress, a tool that explains a texture, a tray of one edition before it is dispersed. Use that frame on a page about the studio, or low on the piece page, after the clean product views. The grid stays clean so the silhouettes compare.

Hands should be steady and ordinary. No performance of "artisan" with flourishes that obscure the piece. If your hands are in the scale shot, keep skin tones natural and the grip loose enough to see the object. Crop out the clutter of the studio unless the clutter is the point of a single behind-the-work picture.

Packaging gets one frame if it matters to the gift: the box closed, then the piece inside, same light as the product shots. Do not build a second aesthetic for the unboxing. People will screenshot whatever you give them and compare it to the product tile. Those two images should look like the same studio on the same day.

If you repair work, a before-and-after belongs on a repair page, with the client's piece shown only when you have permission. Do not use a customer's ring as a product photo. That is a different object, and it is not yours to sell.

## Crop, ground, and metal color

Pick the ground once. A light gray, a warm paper, a quiet stone. It has to let both yellow gold and silver read. A background that flatters only one metal will distort the other, and your grid will split in two.

The crop for the grid should place every piece in the same region of the frame, with a similar margin. Rings look larger than pendants if you fill the frame with each. Decide whether the frame is "object fills seventy percent" or "object sits at true relative scale." Relative scale is harder and often clearer. Filling the frame is easier and needs the scale shot on every page. Either system works. Mixing them does not.

Light from a consistent side so highlights land in the same place. Metal is a mirror. Inconsistent light is inconsistent color. Save a white balance for the ground you chose, and photograph a gray card at the start of the session if your camera drifts.

Color-check against the real piece at the door of the studio, in daylight, before you publish. Screens lie. If the gold in the file is orange and the gold in your hand is pale, correct the file or reshoot. This is the step that keeps a careful studio from looking cheap online, and it takes ten minutes.

File names should include the piece name and the view: whole, detail, scale. You will hand these to a developer or drop them into a shop admin months later. "DSC_4412" is how the wrong angle becomes the thumbnail.

## A set you can finish

For each piece:

1. Whole piece on the shared ground, shared crop.
2. One detail that answers the question a buyer would zoom for.
3. One scale frame using the reference you always use.
4. A variant only when the variant looks different.

Reject soft focus, fingerprints, clipped highlights on the prongs, and any frame with a different background. Delete them in the session. A rejects folder becomes a backup people publish by accident.

Alt text must carry the facts the picture is for. Under the [W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/), information in an image needs a text alternative so the content is perceivable. "Gold ring" is not enough if the page is about a narrow recycled band. Name the metal, the type of object, and the view: "Recycled yellow gold band, whole piece, on the studio gray." The scale frame should say it is on a hand. The detail should say what the detail is.

Check a row of eight on a phone. If one piece looks larger only because the crop is tighter, reshoot it. If one metal looks dirty only because the white balance drifted, correct the set, not the single favorite. The grid is the unit.

A consistent object picture is a product decision. The next decision is whether the site around those pictures should live in a page builder or in custom code, which depends on who will edit it and what the pages have to do. That piece is [custom site or a page builder](/blog/custom-site-or-a-page-builder).
